name: Mew family orthotropic clinics (Mike & John Mew)

image.caption: Mew family orthotropic clinics (Mike & John Mew)

lead: The Mew family clinics are the practices where John Mew, and later his son Mike Mew, applied orthotropics, an approach to dental and facial development that treats crooked teeth and a recessed jaw as results of posture. Patients, many of them children, were offered palatal expanders and training to hold the tongue against the roof of the mouth, with the stated aim of a broader upper jaw, better-aligned teeth and a more forward, defined facial structure.

The approach became the origin of "mewing", the do-it-yourself tongue-posture practice popular in looksmaxxing circles from 2019. Published reviews describe the evidence for orthotropics as inadequate, and the UK General Dental Council took regulatory action against both Mews over the years.

paras: In the clinic model, a practitioner assessed a patient's facial profile and bite, then prescribed appliances such as palatal expanders, advice on chewing and diet, and a tongue-resting posture to be maintained throughout the day. Treatment was most often discussed for children whose faces were still growing. Online, the same ideas were spread through Mike Mew's YouTube videos.

A General Dental Council panel found in 2024 that Mike Mew had used approaches not sufficiently supported by scientific evidence and liable to cause harm, and erased him from the register. John Mew's licence was revoked in 2017. Orthodontic bodies do not regard orthotropics as an alternative to standard orthodontics or jaw surgery.

angle.text: The clinics offered treatment intended to change facial structure, mainly in growing children, by widening the upper jaw and training the tongue to rest against the palate. The same ideas fed the DIY mewing trend among adults seeking a sharper jawline.

lead: The Mew family orthotropic clinics were the dental practices of British orthodontist John Mew (1928-2025) and his son Michael (Mike) Mew, in which they offered orthotropics, a method of guiding facial growth through appliances, tongue posture and diet. Proponents present it as a way to widen the jaws and align the teeth so the face develops with a more prominent, defined structure, an outcome that is directly about appearance [1].

John Mew proposed the "Tropic Premise" in 1958, treating malocclusion as a postural problem, and co-founded the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance in 1987 [2]. His method used palatal expanders, dietary changes and tongue training [2]. His son Mike continued the work and became its public face through YouTube, and the do-it-yourself tongue posture practice named after the family, mewing, gained wide social-media attention from 2019 [1][3].

Mainstream orthodontists opposed the approach, and published commentary describes the evidence as inadequate [1]. The General Dental Council (GDC) reprimanded John Mew in 2010 over misleading advertisements and revoked his licence in 2017 [1][2]. Mike Mew was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society and, after a misconduct tribunal, was erased from the dental register in November 2024 [3][4].

paras: Orthotropics holds that the shape of the face and the alignment of the teeth are largely determined by environmental factors such as resting tongue position, breathing and chewing, rather than mainly by genetics. John Mew argued that malocclusion is a postural deformity, in contrast to mainstream orthodontics, which attributes crooked teeth mainly to genetic factors [2]. He also held that extractions, fixed braces, elastics and headgear could harm facial growth [1].

In the clinic setting, treatment combined palatal expanders that widen and advance the upper jaw, advice on diet, and tongue posture training [2]. Patients were frequently children, since the approach is aimed at guiding growth.

John Mew was born in 1928 in Royal Tunbridge Wells, qualified in dentistry at University College London in 1953 and gained a specialty qualification in orthognathic surgery in 1956 [2]. He put forward the Tropic Premise in 1958 and in 1968 met Rolf Fränkel, who introduced him to the work of Konstantin Buteyko [1]. He co-founded the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance in Fort Worth, Texas in 1987 [1]. He died on 25 June 2025 at the age of 96 [2].

Mike Mew carried the approach forward as a practitioner and through online video, and the term mewing, derived from the family name, spread on social media from 2019 [1][3]. He was expelled from the British Orthodontic Society around that year and started a petition to reverse the decision [2].

The NHS fined John Mew for inappropriate treatment; he appealed in the High Court in 1987 and won, with costs [2]. In 2010 the GDC reprimanded him for misleading advertisements, a charge he did not dispute while describing himself as a whistleblower [2]. In 2017 the GDC revoked his licence over false advertising and breach of patient confidentiality [2].

Mike Mew faced a GDC misconduct hearing reported in 2022. In November 2024 he was erased from the dentists' register [3][4]. One case involved a six-year-old boy treated in 2018 who was told to wear an expansion device with head and neck gear for long daily periods and who reportedly had prolonged seizure-like episodes [4]. The panel found advice in his YouTube videos misleading and inappropriate [4]. A GDC spokesman said he had used approaches not sufficiently supported by scientific evidence and liable to cause harm [4]. Mike Mew responded that the GDC was more concerned with protecting the orthodontic industry than children [4].

No studies found. A 2019 commentary in the Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery assessed mewing, and Wikipedia's summaries note that no controlled clinical trial supports orthotropics; the American Association of Orthodontists reports no evidence that it improves the jaw [1][3].

Interest in the Mews' ideas rose from January 2019 through social-media virality, particularly in looksmaxxing and related communities [3]. Many followers adopt the free tongue-posture practice rather than attending a clinic.
